newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Music chiefs gear up for cyberspace copyright wars.
newsitem.headline: Music chiefs gear up for cyberspace copyright wars.

text.p: The world's $40 billion-a-year music industry, battling to protect copyrights in the tangled web of Internet, plans electronic tagging to charge listeners in cyberspace, an official said Wednesday.
Music and other copyright-based industries are campaigning for global pacts to sort out who owns what on the Internet and to fight against cyberspace piracy.

At a conference in Geneva, Nicholas Garnett, director-general of the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) lobby group whose 1,100 members include record producers BMG, EMI, MCA, Sony Music and PolyGram, said in an interview that digital era rules between music consumers and producers had to be rewritten.
He said the time was not too far away in the future when recordings would be just a click away on the Internet, but consumers would have to pay the price for copyrighted music.
"You'll be home and have your on-line connection. You'll programme your music for the week and select items from a huge database that'll be fed into your system," Garnett said.

"But we need equal rights in an electronic environment which we have now so we can do business. We'll come up with security systems to prevent piracy. There will be identification tags. Unless you supply the key, no one can listen to music."
Copyright is big business for the world's music industry and the information superhighway is causing some big headaches, challeging traditional notions of reproduction and distribution.

Copyright laws based on national boundaries are irrelevant in the borderless world of the Internet -- a giant copying machine where anything from music to software can be duplicated and distributed at the click of a computer mouse.

The three-week Geneva conference, which began on Monday under the auspices of the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO), a specialised U.N. agency that coordinates international patents and copyrights, will debate three treaties on literary and artistic works, the rights of performers and producers of music and producers of databases.
But copyright experts and negotiators from more than 120 countries have been bogged down in procedures so far and crucial talks on the treaties have yet to begin.

So far, there are more questions than answers: which national laws will apply to infringements, how will copyrights be protected in "haven" countries with no legislation, how will technical protection be ensured against hackers?

Diplomats said the battleline at the negotiating table will be drawn between copyright-based industries and an array of academic, consumer, scientific and technical groups as well as service providers which say the treaties will retard the Internet.
Critics say the proposals will give wide powers to the entertainment industry and put extra burdens on the consumer.
Although the amount of music that goes through the Internet is miniscule so far, Garnett said it is set to grow at a fast rates, along with the cost of cyberspace piracy in lost sales.
Without copyright protection, he said there would be no incentive for electronic delivery of music recordings which he said could represent a $2 billion market in coming years.

If music companies are unable to control piracy off-line, which amounted to losses of at least $2 billion worldwide in 1995, how will they control it on the Internet, where the pirate and the listener can be the same person?

"There are millions of Net users popping up around the world. Although we don't like it, there's no way we can control what members of the public do in their living rooms," Garnett said. "Control is going to be extremely difficult."
